CausalChain: HCC tumor → Elevated PCSK9 expression → (Path 1: Increased degradation of LDLR on tumor cells → Metabolic rewiring: lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, ferroptosis) AND (Path 2: Increased degradation of LDLR on T cells → Impaired TCR recycling → Reduced CD8+ T cell activation) → PCSK9 inhibition restores LDLR function in both compartments → (Path 1: Enhanced ferroptosis and tumor cell death) AND (Path 2: Improved TCR recycling and CD8+ T cell activation) → Synergistic enhancement with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors → Robust antitumor immune response
Hypothesis: In hepatocellular carcinoma, we hypothesize that dual targeting of PCSK9 will yield a two-pronged antitumor strategy. First, PCSK9 inhibition will counteract its tumor cell-autonomous role by enhancing LDLR-mediated lipid uptake, thereby provoking intracellular lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and subsequent ferroptosis. Concurrently, restoring LDLR levels on CD8+ T cells will improve TCR recycling and signaling, leading to enhanced T cell activation. This dual effect is anticipated to synergize with PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint inhibition, ultimately resulting in a more robust antitumor immune response. The hypothesis will be tested employing state-of-the-art methods, including CRISPR/Cas9 mediated gene editing, advanced live-cell imaging of LDLR and TCR dynamics, and single-cell RNA sequencing to resolve compartment-specific effects.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major therapeutic challenge, with emerging evidence implicating PCSK9 in both metabolic regulation and immune modulation. Here, we propose that targeted inhibition of PCSK9 in HCC can simultaneously induce tumor cell metabolic reprogramming—marked by lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis—and restore low‐density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) function in CD8+ T cells, thereby enhancing T-cell receptor (TCR) recycling and activation. Utilizing cutting-edge genomic tools such as CRISPR-Cas9 screens, high-resolution live-cell imaging, and single-cell RNA sequencing, this dual-mechanism approach can be rigorously validated in preclinical models. When combined with PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockade, PCSK9 inhibition is hypothesized to produce synergistic antitumor responses via both direct tumor cytotoxicity and potentiation of adaptive immunity.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis exclusively focused on the immune mechanism whereby PCSK9 inhibition would restore LDLR-mediated TCR recycling on CD8+ T cells to enhance antitumor immunity with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. The revised hypothesis integrates the established metabolic effects—specifically, the induction of lipid metabolic rewiring and ferroptosis in tumor cells—into the causal chain. By explicitly acknowledging PCSK9's dual role in modulating both tumor cell metabolism and T cell function, and by leveraging contemporary technological tools (e.g., CRISPR screens, high-resolution imaging, and single-cell sequencing), the revised hypothesis not only remains true to the original causal reasoning but also broadens its scope, thereby enhancing its practical implementability and scientific rigor.
